sentences.text: In this video, we'll learn the cross product the easy way, and see how meteorology uses it to explain why the wind turns and why storms spin.
What is the cross product?
Let's see what it is, why it's built this way, and what it tells us about the wind.
In the last video, we met the dot product.
We took vector a with components five and one, and vector b with components one and three.
sentences.audio_text: We took vector [A](/ˈA/) with components five and one, and vector b with components one and three.

sentences.text: We found that a dot b equals eight.
sentences.audio_text: We found that [A](/ˈA/) dot b equals eight.

sentences.text: In pictures, it was the shadow of one arrow on the other, times the other arrow's length.
And in weather, v dot grad T told us how fast the wind carries air into warmer or colder places.
It worked on a map of isotherms, the lines of equal temperature.
That's a number, and numbers are great for measuring how much two arrows agree.
But a number can't describe everything.
Imagine pushing a door open.
Draw one arrow from the hinge to your hand, along the door.
Then draw a second arrow for your push.
When you push at a right angle to the door, the dot product of these two arrows is zero.
Yet the door turns the most.
When you push along the door, straight towards the hinge, the dot product is as large as it can be.
Yet the door doesn't turn at all.
So for turning, the dot product gets things backwards.
There's a second problem.
Suppose the wind blows north, and something pushes it sideways.
The push could be to the east, or to the west.
Both pushes are at right angles to the wind, so both dot products are zero.
The dot product gives the same number for a push to the right as for a push to the left.
So it can't tell left from right.
A turning also has an axis: the door swings around the line of its hinge.
So we need a new product, one that's largest at right angles.
It should also give an arrow along an axis.
That's the cross product.
The cross product lives in three dimensions, so let's add a third axis.
Here x points east, y points north, and z points straight up.
The unit vectors along them are called x hat, y hat and z hat.
Each one is one unit long.
Our two arrows lie flat on the floor, so their third components are zero.
Vector a becomes five, one, zero, and vector b becomes one, three, zero.
sentences.audio_text: Vector [A](/ˈA/) becomes five, one, zero, and vector b becomes one, three, zero.

sentences.text: So how do we find the cross product?
The answer is an arrow, so we need three components.
Each one has a recipe.
For the x component, we leave out the x parts, and use only the y and z parts.
We take the y part of vector a times the z part of b.
sentences.audio_text: We take the y part of vector [A](/ˈA/) times the z part of b.

sentences.text: Then we subtract the z part of vector a times the y part of b.
sentences.audio_text: Then we subtract the z part of vector [A](/ˈA/) times the y part of b.

sentences.text: The y component leaves out the y parts and uses z and x.
The z component leaves out the z parts and uses x and y.
Each pair follows the cycle x, y, z, and back to x.
And there's always a minus sign between the two products.
Let's try it on our two arrows.
The x component is one times zero, minus zero times three, which is zero.
The y component is zero times one, minus five times zero, which is also zero.
The z component is five times three, minus one times one.
That's fifteen minus one, which is fourteen.
So a cross b has components zero, zero and fourteen.
sentences.audio_text: So [A](/ˈA/) cross b has components zero, zero and fourteen.

sentences.text: It's an arrow fourteen units long, pointing straight up.
It stands out of the floor where vector a and vector b lie.
sentences.audio_text: It stands out of the floor where vector [A](/ˈA/) and vector b lie.

sentences.text: Because the answer is a vector, the cross product is also called the vector product.
Now let's look at how the angle between the two arrows plays a role.
For the dot product, we multiplied the two lengths by the cosine of theta.
The length of the cross product uses the sine instead.
It's the length of vector a times the length of b, times sine theta.
sentences.audio_text: It's the length of vector [A](/ˈA/) times the length of b, times sine theta.

sentences.text: The sine is zero when two arrows point the same way, and one at a right angle.
It's zero again when they point in opposite directions.
From the last video, the lengths are about five point one and three point one six.
The angle theta is about sixty degrees, with a sine of about point eight seven.
Multiplied out, that's fourteen again.
Now let's find a picture for this number.
In the last video, we dropped a line from the tip of vector a onto b's line.
sentences.audio_text: In the last video, we dropped a line from the tip of vector [A](/ˈA/) onto b's line.

sentences.text: The piece it marked off along b was the shadow.
This time, look at the dropped line itself.
Its length is the height of vector a above b's line.
sentences.audio_text: Its length is the height of vector [A](/ˈA/) above b's line.

sentences.text: That's the length of vector a times sine theta, about four point four three.
sentences.audio_text: That's the length of vector [A](/ˈA/) times sine theta, about four point four three.

sentences.text: Now slide a copy of b to the tip of vector a and a copy of vector a to the tip of b.
sentences.audio_text: Now slide a copy of b to the tip of vector [A](/ˈA/) and a copy of vector [A](/ˈA/) to the tip of b.

sentences.text: Together they make a slanted box called a parallelogram.
Its area is the base times the height.
That's three point one six times four point four three, which is about fourteen.
So the length of a cross b is the area of the parallelogram the two arrows make.
sentences.audio_text: So the length of [A](/ˈA/) cross b is the area of the parallelogram the two arrows make.

sentences.text: The direction is just as neat.
The cross product a cross b is at a right angle to both arrows.
sentences.audio_text: The cross product [A](/ˈA/) cross b is at a right angle to both arrows.

sentences.text: We can check it with the dot product.
A right angle gives a dot product of zero.
Zero times five, plus zero times one, plus fourteen times zero, is zero.
The same happens with b.
But there are two directions at right angles to the floor: up and down.
Which one does the cross product choose?
That's what the right-hand rule tells us.
Hold out your right hand.
Point your fingers along vector a so they follow the first arrow.
sentences.audio_text: Point your fingers along vector [A](/ˈA/) so they follow the first arrow.

sentences.text: Now curl your fingers towards b, the second arrow, the short way round.
Your thumb now points along a cross b: straight up.
sentences.audio_text: Your thumb now points along [A](/ˈA/) cross b: straight up.

sentences.text: Let's walk around it.
From every side, the curl, the thumb and the arrow agree.
There's a second way to use the same hand.
Point your index finger along vector a and your middle finger along b.
sentences.audio_text: Point your index finger along vector [A](/ˈA/) and your middle finger along b.

sentences.text: Bend the middle finger away from your palm.
Then stick your thumb straight up.
Your thumb again points along a cross b.
sentences.audio_text: Your thumb again points along [A](/ˈA/) cross b.

sentences.text: So the index finger is the first arrow, and the middle finger is the second.
The thumb is the answer.
A third way uses a bottle cap, or a screw.
Turn the cap from vector a towards b, the short way round.
sentences.audio_text: Turn the cap from vector [A](/ˈA/) towards b, the short way round.

sentences.text: Seen from above, that's anticlockwise, the way you open a bottle.
And the cap rises, up along a cross b.
sentences.audio_text: And the cap rises, up along [A](/ˈA/) cross b.

sentences.text: Turn it back the other way, from b towards the first arrow.
Then the cap screws down, the way a bottle closes.
A screw works the same way.
Turned from the first arrow towards the second, it moves along their cross product.
Now let's use the rule on the three axes themselves.
Point your fingers along x hat and curl them towards y hat.
Your thumb points up, so x hat cross y hat is z hat.
Now turn your hand so your fingers point along y hat.
Then curl them towards z hat.
Your thumb points along x hat, so y hat cross z hat is x hat.
Turn it once more, with your fingers along z hat, curling towards x hat.
Your thumb points along y hat.
So z hat cross x hat is y hat.
The three results follow a cycle: x, y, z, and back to x.
What if we swap the order?
Point your fingers along y hat first, and curl them towards x hat.
To curl that way, you have to turn your hand over.
Your thumb now points down.
So y hat cross x hat is minus z hat.
In the same way, z hat cross y hat is minus x hat.
And x hat cross z hat is minus y hat.
And b cross a has components zero, zero and minus fourteen.
sentences.audio_text: And b cross [A](/ˈA/) has components zero, zero and minus fourteen.

sentences.text: It has the same length, but points straight down.
In general, swapping the order of a cross product flips its arrow.
That's different from the dot product, where a dot b equals b dot a.
sentences.audio_text: That's different from the dot product, where [A](/ˈA/) dot b equals b dot [A](/ˈA/).

sentences.text: Let's see all six results on a flat screen, with x pointing right and y pointing up.
Then z points straight out of the screen, towards you.
An arrow coming out of the screen is drawn as a dot in a circle, like the tip of an arrow flying at you.
An arrow going into the screen is drawn as a cross in a circle.
It's like the tail feathers of an arrow flying away.
First, x hat cross y hat comes out of the screen.
And y hat cross x hat goes into it.
Next, y hat cross z hat points right, and z hat cross y hat points left.
And z hat cross x hat points up, and x hat cross z hat points down.
So the cross product can point up or down, left or right, into or out of the screen.
The right hand always tells us which.
The direction also depends on where you look from.
Look down at the floor from above.
Turning from vector a to b is anticlockwise, and a cross b points up, straight at you.
sentences.audio_text: Turning from vector [A](/ˈA/) to b is anticlockwise, and [A](/ˈA/) cross b points up, straight at you.

sentences.text: Now look up from below the floor.
The very same turn now looks clockwise, and the same arrow points away from you.
From the side, you see it standing straight up.
So here's a handy rule.
If, from where you stand, the turn from the first arrow to the second is anticlockwise, the cross product points towards you.
If it's clockwise, it points away.
Now let's keep one arrow fixed and change only the other one.
We did the same for the dot product.
The fixed arrow, p, has components three, zero and zero.
First, q points in the same direction as p, with components two, zero and zero.
The parallelogram is squashed flat and has no area.
That makes p cross q zero.
In the next case, q is at a right angle to p.
Its components are zero, two and zero.
Now the parallelogram is a rectangle, three by two.
And p cross q points straight up, six units long.
Last, q points in the opposite direction, with components minus two, zero and zero.
The parallelogram is flat again, so the cross product is zero.
In general, when two vectors point the same way or in opposite directions, their cross product is zero.
And when they're at right angles, it's as long as it can be.
If q keeps turning, past the opposite direction, the turn from p to q becomes clockwise.
Then the arrow flips to point down.
Let's put the two products side by side.
The dot product gives a number, and the cross product gives an arrow.
The dot product uses the cosine of the angle.
The cross product uses the sine.
In pictures, the dot product is a shadow times a length.
The length of the cross product is an area.
The dot product is largest when the arrows point the same way.
The cross product is largest when they're at right angles.
Swapping the order doesn't change the dot product, but it flips the cross product.
In mechanics, the dot product gives work.
The cross product gives torque, which we'll meet next.
And in weather, the dot product gives advection.
The cross product turns the wind, as we'll see soon.
Now let's see why physics needs the cross product.
Imagine turning a bolt with a spanner.
Draw an arrow, r, from the bolt to your hand, zero point three metres long.
Then draw an arrow, F, for your push of fifty newtons.
The turning effect of a force is called torque, written tau.
It's the cross product of r with F: tau equals r cross F.
Push at a right angle, and the size of the torque is zero point three times fifty times sine ninety degrees.
That's fifteen newton metres.
Push at thirty degrees to the spanner, and the sine is one half.
The torque drops to seven point five newton metres.
Push along the spanner, and the torque is zero: the bolt doesn't turn.
The torque arrow points along the bolt's axis.
The right-hand rule tells us which way the bolt turns.
Curl your fingers from r towards F.
If your thumb points down into the nut, the bolt tightens, and if it points up, the bolt loosens.
Seen from above, a clockwise turn makes the arrow point down, away from you.
So the cross product tells us both how strongly a force turns something, and which way.
Now back to the door.
With the cross product, a push at right angles to the door gives the largest torque.
A push along the door gives none, just as our hands tell us.
And the torque arrow points along the hinge.
It points up when the door swings one way, and down when it swings the other.
So the cross product does what the dot product couldn't.
It's largest at right angles, and it tells left from right.
In weather, we need one particular cross product again and again.
Meteorologists usually write a wind that blows flat along the ground as u.
So we'll use u from now on, instead of the v of the last video.
On a map, let k be the unit vector pointing straight up, out of the ground.
Take a wind blowing east at five metres per second.
Its components are five, zero and zero.
Then k cross u has components zero, five and zero: it points north.
The wind arrow has been turned ninety degrees to the left.
Its length hasn't changed.
Try a wind blowing north.
Now k cross u points west, again ninety degrees to the left.
So k cross is a turning tool: it turns any flat arrow a quarter turn to the left, anticlockwise seen from above.
sentences.audio_text: So k cross is a turning tool: it turns any flat arrow [A](/ˈA/) quarter turn to the left, anticlockwise seen from above.

sentences.text: And minus k cross u turns it a quarter turn to the right.
Now let's see why the wind needs turning.
Earth spins once a day around the axis through its poles.
We can draw this spin as an arrow, Omega, along the axis.
The right-hand rule picks its direction.
Curl your fingers the way Earth turns, from west to east, and your thumb points to the North Pole.
Its length is how fast Earth turns.
A full turn is two pi radians, the angle unit of calculus.
Measured against the distant stars, one turn takes twenty three hours and fifty six minutes.
That's a little less than a day.
So Omega is about seven point two nine times ten to the minus five radians per second.
Every point on the ground is carried round by this spin.
Draw an arrow, r, from Earth's centre to that point.
Earth's radius is about six thousand three hundred and seventy one kilometres.
The point's velocity is then Omega cross r, another cross product.
At the equator, r is at a right angle to Omega, so the speed is as large as it can be.
It's about four hundred and sixty five metres per second, faster than the speed of sound.
At forty five degrees north, the angle is smaller.
The speed there is about three hundred and twenty nine metres per second.
At the poles, r points along Omega, so the cross product is zero.
There, the ground just turns on the spot.
Now imagine air moving across this spinning ground.
We stand on Earth and turn with it.
So we judge the air's motion against the turning ground.
Seen this way, moving air drifts sideways.
It's as if a force pushed it at a right angle to its motion.
This apparent push is called the Coriolis effect.
sentences.audio_text: This apparent push is called the Cor-ee-oh-liss effect.

sentences.text: In the Northern Hemisphere, the half of Earth north of the equator, it turns moving air to the right.
In the Southern Hemisphere, it turns it to the left.
Where it comes from needs the maths of spinning frames.
It gets its own video later in this series.
Here's what it looks like as maths.
The Coriolis effect adds a push of minus two Omega cross u for each kilogram of air, where u is the wind.
sentences.audio_text: The Cor-ee-oh-liss effect adds a push of minus two Omega cross u for each kilogram of air, where u is the wind.

sentences.text: Because it's a cross product, this push is always at a right angle to the wind.
So its dot product with the wind is zero.
It does no work, and it never speeds the wind up or slows it down.
It only turns it.
For winds that blow flat along the ground, only part of Omega matters.
It's the shadow of Omega on the local up direction, k.
Phi is the latitude, the angle north of the equator.
Between Omega and k, the angle is ninety degrees minus phi.
So the shadow is Omega times sine phi, a dot product again.
Twice this shadow has its own name, the Coriolis parameter, f: f equals two Omega sine phi.
sentences.audio_text: Twice this shadow has its own name, the Cor-ee-oh-liss parameter, f: f equals two Omega sine phi.

sentences.text: At forty five degrees north, f is about one point zero three times ten to the minus four per second.
At the equator, the shadow is zero, so f is zero.
South of the equator, the latitude counts as negative.
So sine phi and f are negative too.
So, for flat winds, the Coriolis push becomes minus f times k cross u.
sentences.audio_text: So, for flat winds, the Cor-ee-oh-liss push becomes minus f times k cross u.

sentences.text: Now the turning tool does its job.
The term k cross u is the wind turned a quarter turn to the left.
The minus sign flips it to the right.
In the Northern Hemisphere, f is positive.
So the push points to the right of the wind.
In the Southern Hemisphere, f is negative, which flips it once more, to the left.
At the equator, f is zero, and there's no turning at all.
How strong is it?
Take a wind of ten metres per second at forty five degrees north.
The push is f times the wind speed: one point zero three times ten to the minus four, times ten.
That's about one millimetre per second, every second.
That's tiny, but it never stops.
If nothing else pushed the air, it would turn the wind round a full circle.
That takes two pi over f, about seventeen hours.
Let's watch this on the globe.
Here are two air parcels, one at forty five degrees north and one at forty five degrees south.
Both are set moving towards the east at ten metres per second, with nothing else pushing them.
The northern one curves to the right, and the southern one curves to the left.
Both trace loops about two hundred kilometres across, turning in opposite directions.
Now let's look at real winds.
These come from a reanalysis: a best estimate of the weather everywhere, on a regular grid.
It's made by combining millions of measurements with a weather forecast model.
Let's average them over the thirty years from nineteen ninety one to twenty twenty.
Near the ground, they show a clear pattern.
Around thirty degrees north and south sit belts of high pressure.
They're called the subtropical highs.
Air flows out of these highs towards the equator.
In the Northern Hemisphere, that air heads south, and the Coriolis effect turns it to the right, towards the west.
sentences.audio_text: In the Northern Hemisphere, that air heads south, and the Cor-ee-oh-liss effect turns it to the right, towards the west.

sentences.text: So it blows from the north east.
In the Southern Hemisphere, it heads north and is turned to the left, again towards the west.
So it blows from the south east.
These steady winds are the trade winds, which sailing ships once used to cross the oceans.
Over the oceans at fifteen degrees north and south, they blow towards the west at about five to seven metres per second.
Let's fly over the Atlantic, and then over the Pacific.
Over both oceans, the winds on either side of the equator lean towards the west.
Air also flows out of the subtropical highs towards the poles.
In the Northern Hemisphere, it heads north and is turned to the right, towards the east.
In the Southern Hemisphere, it heads south and is turned to the left, again towards the east.
These are the westerlies, named, like all winds, after the direction they blow from.
At forty five degrees north and south, they blow towards the east at about three to seven and a half metres per second.
They're strongest over the Southern Ocean, where there's little land to slow them down.
This is a simple picture.
Pressure patterns and friction shape the winds too.
But the Coriolis turning is why they blow mostly east or west, rather than straight north or south.
sentences.audio_text: But the Cor-ee-oh-liss turning is why they blow mostly east or west, rather than straight north or south.

sentences.text: The cross product also explains why storms spin.
A hurricane is a huge storm, hundreds of kilometres across.
It forms over warm ocean, around a centre of very low pressure.
Air near the surface is pushed towards that low centre from every side.
This is Hurricane Ian, seen from a weather satellite on the twenty eighth of September, twenty twenty two.
Its calm centre, called the eye, is just off the south west coast of Florida.
Its cloud bands curl around the eye.
That afternoon, Ian reached the coast with winds of about sixty seven metres per second.
That's the forecasters' best estimate, made from the observations.
Now let's add the winds near the ground, from a weather model with a fine, three kilometre grid.
In the Northern Hemisphere, each stream of air heading for the centre is turned to the right.
Air coming from the south is turned towards the east.
And air coming from the east is turned towards the north.
All the way round, these turned streams add up to an anticlockwise spin, seen from above.
Near the ground, friction slows the wind.
So the air still spirals inwards as it turns.
Now the Southern Hemisphere.
This is Cyclone Idai, seen from a satellite on the fourteenth of March, twenty nineteen.
sentences.audio_text: This is Cyclone Ee-dye, seen from a satellite on the fourteenth of March, twenty nineteen.

sentences.text: It sits in the channel between Mozambique and Madagascar.
Its cloud bands curl the other way.
In this part of the world, storms like this are called cyclones.
Near its peak, its winds reached about fifty four to fifty nine metres per second, again from the forecasters' best estimates.
Here f is negative, so air heading for the centre is turned to the left.
The storm spins clockwise, seen from above.
It's the same physics, with the opposite sign of f.
The cross product can even measure the spin for us.
At each point around the storm, draw an arrow r from the centre to the point.
Then take r cross u with the wind there.
If the wind goes round anticlockwise, seen from above, the turn from r to u is anticlockwise too.
Then the right-hand rule makes r cross u point up.
For Ian, the arrows point up all the way round.
For Idai, they point down: clockwise, seen from above.
sentences.audio_text: For Ee-dye, they point down: clockwise, seen from above.

sentences.text: So both storms spin the way the Coriolis effect turns the air.
sentences.audio_text: So both storms spin the way the Cor-ee-oh-liss effect turns the air.

sentences.text: They spin anticlockwise in the north, and clockwise in the south.
Now the last application: how the wind blows around highs and lows.
Air presses on everything around it.
This pressure is measured in hectopascals.
At sea level, it's about a thousand hectopascals.
On a weather map, we join the places with the same pressure.
We did the same with temperature in the last video.
These lines are called isobars.
Like grad T, grad p points the way the pressure increases fastest.
It points straight across the isobars, towards high pressure.
Air is pushed the other way, from high pressure towards low.
This push, for each kilogram of air, is minus one over rho times grad p.
Here rho is the density of the air: about one point two kilograms per cubic metre.
Let's follow an air parcel that starts at rest between a high and a low.
The pressure push starts it moving towards the low.
But as soon as it moves, the Coriolis effect turns it to the right.
sentences.audio_text: But as soon as it moves, the Cor-ee-oh-liss effect turns it to the right.

sentences.text: The faster it goes, the stronger the turning push.
Soon the parcel blows along the isobars.
In fact, it overshoots and makes a series of loops.
But on average, it moves along the isobars.
Along that average path, the two pushes are equal and opposite.
The pressure push points towards the low, and the Coriolis push points towards the high.
sentences.audio_text: The pressure push points towards the low, and the Cor-ee-oh-liss push points towards the high.

sentences.text: This balance is called geostrophic balance, and the wind it gives is the geostrophic wind.
sentences.audio_text: This balance is called jee-oh-strof-ic balance, and the wind it gives is the jee-oh-strof-ic wind.

sentences.text: In the Northern Hemisphere, it blows with low pressure on its left.
Written as maths, the balance says that f times k cross u equals minus one over rho times grad p.
We want the wind itself, so we apply k cross to both sides.
Turning the wind twice to the left points it backwards.
So k cross k cross u is minus u.
Dividing by f and rho, we get the geostrophic wind.
sentences.audio_text: Dividing by f and rho, we get the jee-oh-strof-ic wind.

sentences.text: The wind u equals one over f rho, times k cross grad p.
Let's read it piece by piece.
Grad p points across the isobars, towards high pressure.
Then k cross turns it a quarter turn to the left, so the wind blows along the isobars.
High pressure is on its right, and low pressure is on its left.
One over f rho sets the speed.
The closer the isobars, the steeper the pressure, and the stronger the wind.
And near the equator, f goes to zero, so this balance breaks down there.
Let's put in numbers.
Suppose the pressure drops by four hectopascals over four hundred kilometres, going north.
We're at forty five degrees north.
Four hectopascals is four hundred pascals.
So the pressure gradient is four hundred pascals over four hundred thousand metres: ten to the minus three pascals per metre.
Next, we multiply f by rho: one point zero three times ten to the minus four, times one point two.
That's about one point two four times ten to the minus four.
Dividing, the wind speed is about eight point one metres per second.
The units work out.
A pascal is a kilogram per metre per second squared, and what's left is metres per second.
And since the low pressure lies to the north, the wind blows east, with the low on its left, just like the westerlies.
Now let's test it on a real storm.
This is Storm Ciarán, a deep low that crossed the North Atlantic.
sentences.audio_text: This is Storm Keer-awn, a deep low that crossed the North Atlantic.

sentences.text: It reached England and France in early November twenty twenty three.
Here it is early on the second of November.
The isobars are drawn every four hectopascals, and they circle the low.
Near the ground, friction disturbs the wind.
So let's look about one and a half kilometres up, where the air feels almost no friction.
The violet arrows are the geostrophic wind at that height.
sentences.audio_text: The violet arrows are the jee-oh-strof-ic wind at that height.

sentences.text: We worked them out with our formula, from the pressure pattern there.
They run along the isobars, anticlockwise round the low.
The low is always on their left.
Where the isobars crowd together, the arrows are longest.
Now let's add the real winds at the same height, from the reanalysis.
They're drawn in a second colour.
Over the sea, they match the geostrophic arrows to within a few per cent in speed, and a few degrees in direction.
sentences.audio_text: Over the sea, they match the jee-oh-strof-ic arrows to within a few per cent in speed, and a few degrees in direction.

sentences.text: Down near the ground, it's different.
Friction slows the air and turns it across the isobars, by about thirteen to twenty one degrees, towards the low.
So from nothing more than a pressure map and a cross product, we get the direction of the wind above the ground.
And we get its speed to within a few per cent.
To sum up, the cross product of two arrows is another arrow, at right angles to both.
Each component leaves out its own direction, and cross multiplies the other two.
There's a minus sign between them.
Its length is the two lengths times sine theta: the area of their parallelogram.
The right-hand rule gives its direction, and swapping the order flips it.
When the arrows point the same way or in opposite directions, it's zero.
At right angles, it's as long as it can be.
